footnotes.text: In the old days people said: It is a pity that things in the world do not go as the pastor preaches. Perhaps the time will come, especially with the help of philosophy, when one can say: Fortunately things do not go as the pastor preaches; for in life there is at least a little meaning, but in his sermon there is none at all.

footnotes.danishText: I gamle Dage sagde man: det er sørgeligt, at det ikke gaaer til i Verden som Præsten prædiker — maaskee kommer den Tid, især ved Philosophiens Hjælp, da man kan sige: heldigviis gaaer det ikke saaledes til som Præsten prædiker; thi i Livet er der dog lidt Mening, i hans Præken er der slet ingen.

footnotes.anchorAfterEn: impossible for it to be translated out of ideality into reality.
footnotes.text: It goes without saying that any other interest in which an individual has concentrated for himself the whole reality of actuality can, when it proves unrealizable, give occasion for the movement of resignation. I have, however, chosen a case of falling in love to display the movements on, because this interest will be easier to understand, and so it spares me all preliminary considerations, which in a deeper sense could occupy only very few people.
footnotes.danishAnchorAfter: sig oversætte fra Idealiteten til Realiteten.
footnotes.danishText: Det følger af sig selv, at hvilkensomhelst anden Interesse, i hvilken et Individ har hele Virkelighedens Realitet for sig concentreret, kan, naar den viser sig urealisabel, foranledige Resignationens Bevægelse. Jeg har imidlertid valgt en Forelskelse til at vise Bevægelserne paa, fordi denne Interesse vil lettere forstaaes, og saaledes fritager mig for alle foreløbige Overveielser, der i dybere Forstand kun kunne beskjæftige ganske Enkelte.

footnotes.anchorAfterEn: everything depends on the movement taking place in the proper way.
footnotes.text: This requires passion. Every movement of infinity takes place through passion, and no reflection is able to produce a movement. It is this perpetual leap in existence that accounts for the movement, while mediation (Hegel’s term for reconciling opposites in a higher unity) is a chimera: in Hegel it is meant to account for everything, and at the same time it is the one thing he has never attempted to account for. Passion is needed even to draw the well-known Socratic distinction between what one understands and what one does not — and still more, of course, to make the true Socratic movement, that of ignorance. But what the age lacks is not reflection but passion. That is why, in a certain sense, the age actually clings to life too stubbornly to die; for to die is among the most curious of leaps. A little verse by a poet has always appealed to me greatly, because after five or six preceding lines in which he has wished himself good things in life, beautifully and simply, he ends like this: ein seliger Sprung in die Ewigkeit — a blessed leap into eternity.
footnotes.danishAnchorAfter: det om, at Bevægelsen skeer normalt.
footnotes.danishText: Dertil hører der Lidenskab. Enhver Uendelighedens Bevægelse skeer ved Lidenskab, og ingen Reflexion kan tilveiebringe en Bevægelse. Dette er det idelige Spring i Tilværelsen, der forklarer Bevægelsen, medens Mediationen er en Chimaire, som hos Hegel skal forklare Alt, og som tillige er det Eneste, han aldrig har forsøgt at forklare. Selv til at gjøre den bekjendte socratiske Distinction mellem hvad man forstaaer og hvad man ikke forstaaer, hører der Lidenskab, end mere naturligviis til at gjøre den egentlige socratiske Bevægelse, Uvidenhedens. Men det, Tiden mangler, er ikke Reflexion, men Lidenskab. Derfor er Tiden egentlig i en vis Forstand for seiglivet til at døe; thi det at døe er et af de mærkeligste Spring, og et lille Vers af en Digter har altid tiltalt mig meget, fordi han, efter i en 5, 6 foregaaende Linier smukt og eenfoldigt at have ønsket sig gode Ting i Livet, ender saaledes: ein seliger Sprung in die Ewigkeit.

footnotes.anchorAfterEn: what unites all human life is passion,
footnotes.text: Lessing has somewhere said something similar from a purely aesthetic standpoint. What he actually wants to show in that passage is that grief, too, can find witty expression. To that end he quotes a remark made in a particular situation by the unhappy English king Edward II. In contrast to this, he cites, following Diderot, a story about a peasant woman and a remark of hers. He then continues: "Auch das war Witz, und noch dazu Witz einer Bäuerin: aber die Umstände machten ihn unvermeidlich. Und folglich auch muss man die Entschuldigung der witzigen Ausdrücke des Schmerzes und der Betrübniss nicht darin suchen, dass die Person, welche sie sagt, eine vornehme, wohlerzogene, verständige, und auch sonst witzige Person sey; denn die Leidenschaften machen alle Menschen wieder gleich: sondern darin, dass wahrscheinlicher Weise ein jeder Mensch ohne Unterschied in den nämlichen Umständen das nämliche sagen würde. Den Gedanken der Bäuerin hätte eine Königin haben können und haben müssen: so wie das, was dort der König sagt, auch ein Bauer hätte sagen können und ohne Zweifel würde gesagt haben." [That too was wit, and a peasant woman's wit at that; but the circumstances made it unavoidable. And consequently the excuse for witty expressions of pain and grief must not be sought in the fact that the person who says them is a distinguished, well-bred, intelligent and otherwise witty person; for the passions make all human beings equal again. It must be sought in the fact that, in all probability, every human being without distinction would say the same thing in the same circumstances. A queen could have had, and must have had, the peasant woman's thought, just as what the king says there a peasant too could have said, and no doubt would have said.] Cf. Sämtliche Werke, vol. 30, p. 223.

footnotes.danishText: Lessing har etsteds yttret noget Lignende fra et reent æsthetisk Standpunkt. Han vil egentlig paa det Sted vise, at Sorgen ogsaa kan give sig et vittigt Udtryk. Han anfører til den Ende en Replik i en bestemt Situation af den ulykkelige engelske Konge Edvard, den Anden. I Modsætning dertil anfører han, efter Diderot, en Fortælling om en Bondekone og en Replik af hende. Nu vedbliver han: Auch das war Witz, und noch dazu Witz einer Bäuerin: aber die Umstände machten ihn unvermeidlich. Und folglich auch muss man die Entschuldigung der witzigen Ausdrücke des Schmerzes und der Betrübniss nicht darin suchen, dass die Person, welche sie sagt, eine vornehme, wohlerzogene, verständige, und auch sonst witzige Person sey; denn die Leidenschaften machen alle Menschen wieder gleich: sondern darin, dass wahrscheinlicher Weise ein jeder Mensch ohne Unterschied in den nämlichen Umständen das nämliche sagen würde. Den Gedanken der Bäuerin hätte eine Königin haben können und haben müssen: so wie das, was dort der König sagt, auch ein Bauer hätte sagen können und ohne Zweifel würde gesagt haben. Cfr. Sämtliche W. 30 B. p. 223.

footnotes.anchorAfterEn: truly loves Isaac with all his soul.
footnotes.text: I want to shed light once more on the difference between the collision as it confronts the tragic hero and as it confronts the knight of faith. The tragic hero assures himself that the ethical obligation is wholly present in him by transforming it into a wish. Agamemnon can thus say: "The proof, for me, that I am not violating my duty as a father is that what is my duty is my only wish." So here we have wish and duty facing each other. The happy thing in life is when the two coincide, when my wish is my duty and vice versa, and most people's task in life is precisely to remain in their duty and, by their enthusiasm, to transform it into their wish. The tragic hero gives up his wish in order to fulfill his duty. For the knight of faith, too, wish and duty are identical, but he is required to give up both. So if he wants to resign himself by giving up his wish, he finds no rest; for it is, after all, his duty. If he wants to remain in his duty and in his wish, he does not become the knight of faith; for the absolute duty required precisely that he give it up. The tragic hero received a higher expression of duty, but not an absolute duty.
footnotes.danishAnchorAfter: elsker Isaak af sin ganske Sjæl.
footnotes.danishText: Forskjellen mellem Collisionen, saaledes som denne er sat den tragiske Helt og Troens Ridder, vil jeg endnu engang belyse. Den tragiske Helt forvisser sig om, at den ethiske Forpligtelse er totalt tilstede i ham derved, at han forvandler den til et Ønske. Agamemnon kan saaledes sige: dette er mig Beviset for, at jeg ikke krænker min Faderpligt, at det, der er min Pligt, er mit eneste Ønske. Vi have altsaa her Ønske og Pligt ligeoverfor hinanden. Det Lykkelige i Livet er, at det falder sammen, at mit Ønske er min Pligt og omvendt, og de fleste Menneskers Opgave i Livet er netop at blive i deres Pligt, og at forvandle den ved deres Begeistring til deres Ønske. Den tragiske Helt opgiver sit Ønske for at fuldkomme sin Pligt. For Troens Ridder er Ønske og Pligt ogsaa identiske, men der fordres, at han skal opgive begge Dele. Naar han da vil resignere ved at opgive sit Ønske, da finder han ikke Hvile; thi det er jo hans Pligt. Vil han blive i Pligten og i sit Ønske, da bliver han ikke Troens Ridder; thi den absolute Pligt fordrede netop, at han skulde opgive den. Den tragiske Helt fik et høiere Udtryk af Pligt, men ikke en absolut Pligt.

footnotes.anchorAfterEn: in their anxiety they may discover one thing or another.
footnotes.text: These movements and positions might well still become the object of aesthetic treatment; but whether faith’s movements and positions, and the whole life of faith, can become so, I leave undecided here. Only, since it always gives me joy to thank whomever I owe something, I want to thank Lessing for the scattered hints about a Christian drama that are found in his Hamburgische Dramaturgie (Hamburg Dramaturgy). He, however, fixed his gaze on the purely divine side of this life (the completed victory), and therefore he despaired; perhaps he would have judged otherwise had he paid more attention to the purely human side (theologia viatorum — the theology of those still on the way). What he says is admittedly very brief, and partly evasive; but since I am always exceedingly glad when I can get an occasion to bring Lessing in, I take it at once. Lessing was not only one of the most comprehensive minds Germany has possessed; he not only had a quite rare readiness in his knowledge, which means that one can safely rely on him and on his autopsy — his own firsthand inspection — without fear of being fooled by loose quotations that belong nowhere, by half-understood phrases fetched from unreliable compendia, or of being led astray by a stupid trumpeting of novelties that older writers set out far better — but he also had a most uncommon gift for explaining what he himself had understood. There he stopped; in our time people go further, and explain more than they themselves have understood.
footnotes.danishAnchorAfter: Angst kunne opdage Eet og Andet.
footnotes.danishText: Disse Bevægelser og Stillinger kunne vel endnu blive Gjenstand for æsthetisk Behandling, hvorvidt derimod Troens og hele Troeslivet kan blive det, lader jeg her uafgjort. Kun vil jeg, fordi det altid er mig en Glæde at takke hvem jeg skylder Noget, takke Lessing for de enkelte Vink om et christeligt Drama, der findes i hans hamburgische Dramaturgie. Han har imidlertid hæftet Blikket paa den reen guddommelige Side af dette Liv (den fuldendte Seier), derfor har han mistvivlet; maaskee vilde han have dømt anderledes, hvis han havde været mere opmærksom paa den reen menneskelige Side. (Theologia viatorum). Det, han siger, er unegtelig meget kort, tildeels undvigende, men da jeg altid er saare glad, naar jeg kan faae Leilighed til at tage Lessing med, tager jeg ham strax. Lessing var ikke blot et af de mest omfattende Hoveder, Tydskland har eiet; han var ikke blot i Besiddelse af en ganske sjelden Prompthed i sin Viden, der gjør, at man trygt kan stole paa ham og hans Autopsi uden at frygte for at blive narret ved løse Citater, som intetsteds have hjemme, halvforstaaede Phraser, der ere hentede fra upaalidelige Compendier, eller desorienteret ved en dum Udbasunen af Nyheder, som de Ældre have fremsat langt bedre — men han havde tillige en høist ualmindelig Gave til at forklare, hvad han selv har forstaaet. Derved blev han staaende, i vor Tid gaaer man videre, og forklarer mere end man selv har forstaaet.

footnotes.anchorAfterEn: he will not have the wedding. I need no more.
footnotes.text: According to Aristotle, the historical catastrophe was as follows: to take revenge, the family gets a temple vessel in among his household goods, and he is condemned as a temple robber. This, however, is of no importance; for the question is not whether the family is clever or stupid in taking its revenge. The family has ideal significance only insofar as it is drawn into the hero’s dialectic. Besides, it is fateful enough that, in trying to escape the danger by not marrying, he plunges into it, and that his life touches the divine in two ways: first through the augur’s pronouncement, then by being condemned as a temple robber.
footnotes.danishAnchorAfter: holde Bryllup. Mere behøver jeg ikke.
footnotes.danishText: Den historiske Katastrophe var efter Aristoteles følgende: for at hævne sig skaffer Familien et Tempel-Kar ind blandt hans Huusgeraad, og han bliver dømt som Tempelrøver. Dette er imidlertid ligegyldigt; thi Spørgsmaalet er ikke, om Familien er snild eller dum i at tage Hævn, Familien faaer kun ideal Betydning forsaavidt den drages ind i Heltens Dialektik. Forøvrigt er det skjæbnesvangert nok, at han, idet han vil undflye Faren ved ikke at gifte sig, styrter i den, samt at hans Liv paa en dobbelt Maade kommer i Berøring med det Guddommelige, først ved Augurens Udsagn, dernæst ved at blive dømt som Tempelrøver.

footnotes.anchorAfterEn: in the same style as Axel and Valborg.
footnotes.text: Incidentally, from this point one could set off in another direction of dialectical movements. Heaven foretells a misfortune for him from his marriage. So he could, of course, refrain from holding the wedding without therefore giving up the girl, and live with her in a romantic union that, for the lovers, would be more than reassuring. This, however, contains an offense against the girl, because he does not, in his love for her, express the universal. It would nevertheless be a task both for a poet and for an ethicist who wanted to defend marriage. In general, if poetry became attentive to the religious and to the inwardness of individuality, it would find far more significant tasks than those it busies itself with now. Over and over, after all, one hears this story in poetry: a man is tied to one girl he once loved — or perhaps never properly loved — because now he has seen another girl, who is the ideal. A man gets it wrong in life: the street was right, but it was the wrong house, for across the way, on the second floor, lives the ideal — this, people think, is a task for poetry. A lover has made a mistake: he saw his beloved by lamplight and thought she had dark hair, but look! on closer inspection it was fair — but her sister, she is the ideal. This, people think, is a task for poetry. My opinion is that every such man is a Laban (a boor) who may be unbearable enough in life but ought to be hissed off at once when he tries to make himself important in poetry. Only passion against passion makes a poetic collision, not this clatter of particularities within one and the same passion. If, for instance, a girl in the Middle Ages falls in love and then satisfies herself that earthly love is a sin, and prefers a heavenly love, then there is a poetic collision here, and the girl is poetic, because her life is in the idea.
footnotes.danishAnchorAfter: samme Stiil som Axel og Valborg.
footnotes.danishText: Forøvrigt kunde man fra dette Punkt komme ind i en anden Retning af dialektiske Bevægelser. Himlen forudsiger ham en Ulykke af hans Ægteskab, saa kunde han jo lade være at holde Bryllup, men derfor ikke opgive Pigen, men leve i en romantisk Forbindelse med hende, der for de Elskende var mere end betryggende. Dette indeholder dog en Fornærmelse mod Pigen, fordi han i sin Kjærlighed til hende ikke udtrykker det Almene. Imidlertid var det en Opgave baade for en Digter og for en Ethiker, der vil forsvare Ægteskabet. Overhovedet vilde Poesien, naar den bliver opmærksom paa det Religieuse og Individualitetens Inderlighed, faae langt betydningsfuldere Opgaver end de, med hvilke den nu sysler. Atter og atter hører man jo i Poesien denne Historie; en Mand er bunden til een Pige, som han engang har elsket, eller maaskee aldrig elsket rigtig, thi nu har han seet en anden Pige, som er Idealet. En Mand tager Feil i Livet, Gaden var rigtig, men det var i et forkeert Huus, thi ligeoverfor paa 2den Sal der boer Idealet — det mener man er en Opgave for Poesien. En Elsker har taget Feil, han har seet den Elskede ved Lys og troet hun havde mørke Haar, men see! ved nærmere Eftersyn havde hun blonde — men Søsteren det er Idealet. Det mener man er en Opgave for Poesien. Min Mening er, at enhver saadan Mand er en Laban, der kan være utaalelig nok i Livet, men som øieblikkelig burde pibes ud, naar han vil gjøre sig vigtig i Poesien. Kun Lidenskab mod Lidenskab giver en poetisk Collision, ikke denne Enkelthedernes Rumsteren indenfor den samme Lidenskab. Naar en Pige f. Ex. i Middelalderen efter at have forelsket sig, forvisser sig om, at jordisk Kjærlighed er en Synd, og foretrækker en himmelsk, saa er her en poetisk Collision, og Pigen er poetisk; thi hendes Liv er i Ideen.

footnotes.anchorAfterEn: I have allowed myself a small change
footnotes.text: That legend could also be treated in another way. The merman does not want to seduce Agnete, even though he has seduced many before. He is no longer a merman — or, if you like, he is a poor wretch of a merman who has long been sitting on the bottom of the sea, grieving. Yet he knows, as the legend does teach, that an innocent girl’s love can save him. But his conscience is bad where girls are concerned, and he does not dare approach them. Then he sees Agnete. Many times already, hidden in the reeds, he has watched her walking along the shore. Her beauty, her quiet absorption in herself, hold him captive to her; but all is melancholy in his soul, and no wild lust stirs in it. And when the merman mingles his sigh with the whispering of the reeds, she turns her ear that way, stands still and sinks into dreams — lovelier than any woman, and yet beautiful as a saving angel who inspires trust in the merman. The merman takes courage; he approaches Agnete, he wins her love, he hopes for his salvation. But Agnete was no quiet girl. She was very fond of the roaring of the sea, and the melancholy sigh by the water pleased her only because it made the roaring within her the stronger. She wants to be off, off — to storm wildly out into the infinite with the merman she loves — then she inflames the merman. She scorned his humility; now pride awakes. And the sea roars, and the wave froths, and the merman clasps Agnete in his arms and hurls himself into the abyss with her. He had never been so wild, never so full of craving; for it was through this girl that he had hoped to be saved. He soon grew tired of Agnete; yet her body was never found, for she became a mermaid who tempted men with her songs.
footnotes.danishAnchorAfter: har tilladt mig en lille Forandring
footnotes.danishText: Ogsaa paa en anden Maade kunde man behandle hiint Sagn. Havmanden vil ikke forføre Agnete, om han end har forført Mange tidligere. Han er ingen Havmand mere, eller han er, om man saa vil, en stakkels Havmand, der allerede længe har siddet nede paa Havsens Bund og sørget. Dog veed han, som det jo læres i Sagnet, at han kan frelses ved en uskyldig Piges Kjærlighed. Men han har en ond Samvittighed med Hensyn til Pigerne, og tør ikke nærme sig dem. Da seer han Agnete. Mange Gange har han allerede, skjult i Sivet, seet hende vandre ved Strandbreden. Hendes Skjønhed, hendes stille Syslen med sig selv fængsler ham til hende; men Alt er Veemod i hans Sjæl, ingen vild Lyst rører sig i den. Og naar da Havmanden blander sit Suk i Sivets Hvisken, da vender hun sit Øre derhen, da staaer hun stille og synker hen i Drømme, deiligere end nogen Qvinde og dog skjøn som en frelsende Engel, der indgyder Havmanden Tillid. Havmanden fatter Mod, han nærmer sig Agnete, han vinder hendes Kjærlighed, han haaber sin Frelse. Men Agnete var ingen stille Pige, hun holdt meget af Havets Brusen, og det veemodige Suk ved Søen behagede hende kun, fordi det da brusede stærkere i hendes Indre. Hun vil afsted, afsted, storme vildt vil hun ud i det Uendelige med Havmanden, som hun elsker — da hidser hun Havmanden. Hun forsmaaede hans Ydmyghed, nu vaagner Stoltheden. Og Havet bruser, og Bølgen fraader, og Havmanden omfavner Agnete og styrter sig i Afgrunden med hende. Aldrig havde han været saa vild, aldrig saa attraaende; thi ved denne Pige havde han haabet sin Frelse. Snart blev han træt af Agnete, dog fandt man aldrig hendes Liig; thi hun blev en Havfrue, der fristede Mændene med sine Sange.

footnotes.text: Aesthetics sometimes treats something similar with its usual flirtatious trifling. The merman is saved by Agnete, and it all ends in a happy marriage. A happy marriage! Easy enough. Let ethics give the address at the wedding ceremony, though, and it will be another matter, I think. Aesthetics throws the cloak of love over the merman, and then everything is forgotten. It is also careless enough to think that a marriage goes the way an auction does, where everything is sold in the condition in which it is found when the hammer falls. It only makes sure that the lovers get each other; the rest it does not care about. It ought just to see what happens afterward; but it has no time for that — it is at once in full swing clapping a new pair of lovers together. Aesthetics is the most faithless of all the sciences. Everyone who has truly loved it becomes, in a certain sense, unhappy; but whoever has never loved it is and remains a pecus — a dull beast.
footnotes.danishAnchorAfter: kun fatte, hvori det Grandiose ligger.
footnotes.danishText: Æsthetiken behandler stundom noget Lignende med sin sædvanlige Leflen. Havmanden bliver frelst ved Agnete, og det Hele ender med et lykkeligt Ægteskab. Et lykkeligt Ægteskab! det er nemt nok. Skal derimod Ethiken holde Talen ved Brudevielsen, saa tænker jeg, det bliver en anden Ting. Æsthetiken kaster Kjærlighedens Kaabe over Havmanden, saa er Alt glemt. Den er tillige skjødesløs nok til at mene, at det gaaer til ved et Ægteskab som paa en Auction, hvor Alt sælges i den Stand, i hvilken det ved Hammerslaget befindes. Den sørger blot for, at de Elskende faae hinanden, Resten bryder den sig ikke om. Den skulde bare see, hvad der skeer bag efter; men dertil har den ikke Tid, den er strax i fuld Gang med at klappe et nyt elskende Par sammen. Æsthetiken er den troløseste af alle Videnskaber. Enhver, der ret har elsket den, bliver i en vis Forstand ulykkelig; men den, der aldrig har elsket den, han er og bliver et pecus.

footnotes.anchorAfterEn: anywhere in what has gone before.
footnotes.text: In the foregoing I have deliberately kept out any consideration of the question of sin and its reality. The whole is directed at Abraham, and him I can still reach in immediate categories — that is, to the extent that I can understand him. The moment sin appears, ethics perishes, and it perishes precisely on repentance. For repentance is the highest ethical expression, but precisely as such it is the deepest ethical self-contradiction.
footnotes.danishAnchorAfter: paa noget Punkt i det Foregaaende.
footnotes.danishText: I det Foregaaende har jeg med Flid holdt ethvert Hensyn til Spørgsmaalet om Synden og dens Realitet borte. Det Hele er rettet paa Abraham, og ham kan jeg endnu naae i umiddelbare Kategorier, det vil sige, forsaavidt jeg kan forstaae ham. Saasnart Synden kommer frem, da gaaer Ethiken til Grunde, netop paa Angeren; thi Angeren er det høieste ethiske Udtryk, men netop som saadant den dybeste ethiske Selvmodsigelse.

footnotes.text: This is not believed in our earnest age; and yet it is remarkable enough that even in paganism — which is by its nature more frivolous and less thoroughly reflected — the two true representatives of the Greek view of existence — γνῶθι σαυτόν, “know yourself” — have each in his own way intimated that by going deep into oneself one discovers first and foremost the disposition to evil. That I am thinking of Pythagoras and Socrates I surely need not say.
footnotes.danishAnchorAfter: med Angst og Gru kan opdage,
footnotes.danishText: Dette troer man ikke paa i vor alvorlige Tid, og dog er det mærkeligt nok, at selv i det, ifølge sit Væsen, mere letsindige og mindre gjennemreflekterede Hedenskab, de to egentlige Repræsentanter for den græske Anskuelse af Tilværelsen γνῶθι σαυτόν, hver paa sin Viis have antydet, at man ved at fordybe sig i sig selv først og fremmest opdager Dispositionen til det Onde. At jeg tænker paa Pythagoras og Socrates, behøver jeg vel ikke at sige.

footnotes.text: If one does not want to use a doubter, one could choose a similar figure — an ironist, for example, whose sharp eye has seen to the bottom of the ridiculousness of existence, and whom a secret understanding with the forces of life assures of what the patient wishes. He knows that he has the power of laughter if he wants to use it; he is sure of his victory — indeed, what is more, of his good fortune. He knows that a single voice will be raised to hold him back, but he knows that he is stronger. He knows that one can still, for a moment, get the men to look serious, but he also knows that in secret they long to laugh with him. He knows that one can still, for a moment, get the woman to hold her fan before her eyes when he speaks; but he knows she is laughing behind the fan; he knows the fan is not absolutely opaque; he knows one can write invisible writing on it; he knows that whenever a woman strikes at him with her fan, that is because she has understood him. He knows unerringly how laughter steals into a person and lives there hidden, and how, once it has taken up lodging, it sits lying in wait. Let us picture such an Aristophanes, such a Voltaire, slightly altered: for he is also a sympathetic nature. He loves existence, he loves people, and he knows that even if laughter’s condemnation may perhaps bring up a young generation that is saved, a great many people in the present generation will go under. So he keeps silent, and as far as possible forgets to laugh himself. But dare he keep silent? Perhaps there are quite a few who do not understand at all the difficulty I am speaking of. They probably think it was an admirable magnanimity to keep silent. That is not at all my view. For I think that any such nature, if he has not had the magnanimity to keep silent, is a traitor to existence. So I demand this magnanimity of him; but when he has it, dare he then keep silent? Ethics is a dangerous science, and it may well be that Aristophanes, determined on purely ethical grounds, resolved to let laughter pass judgment on the age that had gone astray. Aesthetic magnanimity cannot help here; for one does not venture such things on the strength of that. If he is to keep silent, he must go into the paradox. — I will hint at one more design: that a person, for example, possesses an explanation of a hero’s life that explains it in a lamentable way, and yet a whole contemporary age rests absolutely secure in this hero without suspecting anything of the kind.
footnotes.danishAnchorAfter: om Faust. Faust er en Tvivler,
footnotes.danishText: Vil man ikke bruge en Tvivler, kunde man vælge en lignende Figur, en Ironiker f. Ex., hvis skarpe Blik fra Grunden af har opdaget Tilværelsens Latterlighed, hvem en hemmelig Forstaaelse med Kræfterne i Livet forvisser om hvad Patienten ønsker. Han veed, at han har Latterens Magt, hvis han vil bruge den, han er sikker paa sin Seier, ja hvad mere er paa sin Lykke. Han veed, der vil opløfte sig en enkelt Stemme, der vil holde igjen, men han veed, han er stærkere, han veed, at man endnu et Øieblik kan bringe Mændene til at synes alvorlige, men han veed ogsaa, at de i Smug længes efter at lee med ham; han veed, at man endnu et Øieblik kan bringe Qvinden til at holde Viften for Øinene, naar han taler, men han veed, at hun leer bag ved Viften, han veed, at Viften er ikke absolut ugjennemsigtig, han veed, at man kan skrive en usynlig Skrift paa den, han veed, at naar en Qvinde slaaer efter ham med Viften, da er det fordi hun har forstaaet ham, han veed ubedragelig Besked om, hvorledes Latteren sniger sig ind og boer skjult i et Menneske, og naar den engang har taget Bolig, sidder paa Luur og venter. Lad os tænke os en saadan Aristophanes, en saadan Voltaire lidt forandret; thi han er tillige en sympathetisk Natur, han elsker Tilværelsen, han elsker Menneskene og han veed, at om end Latterens Fordømmelse maaskee vil opdrage en frelst ung Slægt, saa vil der i den samtidige gaae en Mængde Mennesker til Grunde. Han tier da, og glemmer saavidt muligt selv at lee. Men tør han tie. Maaskee er der Adskillige, der slet ikke forstaae den Vanskelighed, om hvilken jeg taler. De mene nok, at det var en beundringsværdig Høimodighed at tie. Dette er slet ikke min Mening, thi jeg mener, at enhver saadan Natur, hvis han ikke har havt Høimod til at tie, er en Forræder mod Tilværelsen. Jeg fordrer da altsaa denne Høimodighed af ham; men naar han har den, tør han saa tie. Ethiken er en farlig Videnskab, og det var vel muligt, at Aristophanes, bestemmet reen ethisk, har besluttet sig til at lade Latteren dømme den forvildede Tid. Æsthetisk Høimod kan ikke hjælpe; thi paa den Conto vover man ikke Sligt. Skal han tie, saa maa han ind i Paradoxet. — Endnu et Anlæg vil jeg antyde, at f. Ex. et Menneske eier en Forklaring af en Heros's Liv, der paa en sørgelig Maade forklarer dette, og dog hviler en heel Samtid absolut trygt i denne Heros, uden at ane noget Saadant.

footnotes.anchorAfterEn: to hold him up with pathos.
footnotes.text: Which line of Socrates is to be regarded as the decisive one is a matter on which opinions may differ, since in so many ways Plato has made Socrates evaporate into poetry. I propose the following. The death sentence is announced to him; at that very moment he dies, and at that very moment he overcomes death and carries himself through with his famous retort: that he was surprised to have been condemned by a majority of three votes. No loose and idle talk in the marketplace, no foolish remark by an idiot, could he have joked about more ironically than about the death sentence that condemns him — himself — to death.
footnotes.danishAnchorAfter: til pathetisk at holde ham oppe.
footnotes.danishText: Hvilken Replik af Socrates der maa ansees for den afgjørende, derom kunne Meningerne være delte, da Socrates paa saa mange Maader ved Plato er poetisk forflygtiget. Jeg foreslaaer følgende: Dødsdommen bliver ham forkyndt, i samme Øieblik døer han, i samme Øieblik overvinder han Døden og gjennemfører sig selv i det berømte Tilsvar: at det forundrede ham, at han var bleven dømt med en Majoritet af 3 Stemmer. Ingen løs og ledig Tale paa Torvet, ingen taabelig Bemærkning af en Idiot kunde han have spøget mere ironisk med, end med den Dødsdom, der dømmer ham selv fra Livet.

footnotes.anchorAfterEn: precisely in the silence: Abraham cannot speak.
footnotes.text: Insofar as there can be talk of any analogy, Pythagoras’s situation at his death offers one. For he had to carry through, in his last moment, the silence he had always maintained, and therefore he said: It is better to be killed than to speak. Cf. Diogenes, Book 8, § 39.
footnotes.danishAnchorAfter: i Tausheden, Abraham kan ikke tale.
footnotes.danishText: Forsaavidt der kan være Tale om nogen Analogi, afgiver Pythagoras's Døds-Situation en saadan, thi den af ham altid hævdede Taushed maatte han gjennemføre i sit sidste Øieblik, og derfor sagde han: det er bedre at dræbes end at tale. Cfr. Diogenes 8de Bog § 39.
